description: Take the Sydney Harbour Bridge apart piece by piece in 3D, and read the story of the Coathanger: the 503 meter arch, six million rivets, the sword-slashed ribbon, and the bridge that learned to climb.

hotspots.text: One of 28 panels, each 18.28 meters, making up the 503 meter steel arch. The arch alone holds about 39,000 tonnes of the bridge's 52,800 tonnes of steelwork.
hotspots.title: The arch ribs

hotspots.text: A pair of vertical hangers carrying the deck from the arch. The real hangers run from 7.3 meters at the ends to 58.8 meters at the crown.
hotspots.title: The hangers

hotspots.text: One of four main bearings, each carrying about 20,000 tonnes on a 4.2 meter pin, and letting the arch rise or fall 18 centimeters as the steel heats and cools.
hotspots.title: The main bearings

hotspots.text: One of four decorative 89 meter pylons, concrete faced with granite. They are pure decoration: the arch thrust goes into the skewbacks, not the pylons.
hotspots.title: The pylons

hotspots.text: The 49 meter wide deck carried road, rail, cycle and foot traffic. At 48.8 meters it was the widest long-span bridge in the world until 2006.

intro: Sydney's bridge is a 503 meter steel arch held together by six million rivets, opened in 1932 after a guardsman slashed the ribbon with his sword. It carried the city's traffic, starred in a Pixar film, and then people started climbing it for fun.
page_title: Sydney Harbour Bridge: Exploded 3D Model and History | Architectural Atlas

sections.body: By the 1920s Sydney needed a crossing. Chief engineer John Bradfield pushed the harbour bridge scheme through, and the British firm Dorman Long won the contract to build a steel through arch bridge linking the central business district with the North Shore. Construction was completed on 19 January 1932. The opening, on 19 March 1932, produced the bridge's most famous moment before a car had crossed it: as NSW Premier Jack Lang moved to cut the ribbon, Captain Francis de Groot of the paramilitary New Guard rode forward and slashed it with his cavalry sword, declaring the bridge open in the name of the people. Lang cut the real ribbon anyway, and de Groot was fined for offensive behavior.
sections.heading: The Coathanger

sections.body: The arch was built out from both shores at once, two half-arches reaching toward each other over the water, held by wire-rope anchorages cut into the sandstone until they met in the middle. The numbers are industrial poetry: a 503 meter arch span with its crown 134 meters above the sea, 28 arch panels of 18.28 meters, about six million rivets, 52,800 tonnes of steelwork, and four main bearings taking 20,000 tonnes each. The whole steel arch breathes, rising or falling 18 centimeters as Sydney heats and cools. The deck hangs from the arch on vertical hangers, from 7.3 meters long at the ends to 58.8 meters at the crown.
sections.heading: Six million rivets

sections.body: At 49 meters wide the deck was, until 2006, the widest long-span bridge in the world: eight road lanes, two rail tracks, a cycleway and a footway, with 49 meters of clearance for shipping underneath. The four 89 meter pylons flanking the portals are concrete faced with granite and entirely decorative, which never stopped anyone photographing them. The bridge did its job so well that Sydney grew around it, and the arch they call the Coathanger became the city's signature, the steel curve every postcard reaches for.
sections.heading: The widest in the world

sections.body:
The bridge's screen career began at home. In Mission: Impossible 2 (2000) Tom Cruise's Sydney sequences play out against the harbour, with the bridge, the Opera House and Sydney Tower all in frame. Pixar's Finding Nemo (2003) sets its third act in Sydney Harbour, with the bridge visible in the harbour sequences as Marlin and Dory close in on 42 Wallaby Way. And in the credits of Cars 2 (2011), Lightning McQueen and Mater are shown climbing the bridge itself, which by then was something tourists could actually do: BridgeClimb has been taking visitors up the arch since 1998.

The bridge's biggest annual audience needs no ticket. Every New Year's Eve the arch becomes the centerpiece of Sydney's midnight fireworks, the curve of steel lit up for a global television audience. Between the films, the climb and the fireworks, the Coathanger may be the hardest-working piece of infrastructure in popular culture.
